title: From Kazakhstan to Seoul: A Gap Year Conversation

dialogue.speaker: Asel
dialogue.text: You've just come back from six months in South Korea — I'm so jealous. Tell me everything. What surprised you most?

dialogue.speaker: Yerzhan
dialogue.text: Honestly, the thing that hit me first wasn't the food or the technology — it was the attitude towards age and hierarchy. Seniority really matters there. Even a one-year age difference between colleagues affects how you address each other, what you call each other.

dialogue.speaker: Asel
dialogue.text: That's fascinating. How did you feel about it? Did you find it uncomfortable or did you adapt?

dialogue.speaker: Yerzhan
dialogue.text: Both, at different points. At first it felt quite rigid. Coming from a context where we try to be fairly egalitarian with peers, having to use formal honorifics with someone only slightly older felt strange. But I came to appreciate it — it felt like a very deliberate acknowledgement of relationship.

dialogue.speaker: Asel
dialogue.text: That reminds me of something my grandmother says — that we've lost a lot of that in Kazakhstan. We used to have very clear generational language too. In Kazakh, you use different words depending on whether someone is older or younger than you.

dialogue.speaker: Yerzhan
dialogue.text: Exactly. I think I reconnected with something through Korean culture that I'd taken for granted at home. Which is one of the things I didn't expect from the trip — it made me think more about my own culture.

dialogue.speaker: Yerzhan
dialogue.text: The concept of nunchi — I don't know if you've heard of it. It's roughly the ability to read a social situation and respond appropriately without being told what to do. It's considered a crucial social skill. There's no direct equivalent in Kazakh or Russian, but once you understand it, you see it everywhere.

dialogue.speaker: Asel
dialogue.text: That sounds like what anthropologists call a "cultural untranslatable" — a concept so embedded in one culture that it doesn't translate cleanly into another.

dialogue.speaker: Yerzhan
dialogue.text: Exactly. And I think encountering those untranslatables is the real gift of travel. Not the tourist sites, as beautiful as they are — but the concepts. The ideas for which you have no word, but which make you think: why don't we have a word for this?

dialogue.speaker: Asel
dialogue.text: Did you pick up much Korean?

dialogue.speaker: Yerzhan
dialogue.text: Conversational level. Enough to be taken by surprise when I understood a conversation I wasn't supposed to be part of. That was a milestone. But more importantly, attempting the language changed how people responded to me — even a few words opened doors.

dialogue.speaker: Asel
dialogue.text: That's something I've read about — how the effort of speaking someone's language is read as respect, regardless of how fluent you are.

dialogue.speaker: Yerzhan
dialogue.text: Absolutely. One taxi driver in Seoul told me my Korean was terrible — and then spent the whole journey teaching me phrases. It was the best language lesson I've ever had.

dialogue.speaker: Asel
dialogue.text: That's such a beautiful image. Would you go back?

dialogue.speaker: Yerzhan
dialogue.text: I'd move there if I could. But I also don't think you can go back the same way. The first time, everything is a discovery. The second time, you're building on that. Different, but maybe richer.

vocab.definition: a word or title used to show respect, based on social status or age
vocab.example: "In Korean, honorifics are used even between colleagues who differ by one year in age."

vocab.definition: believing in and working towards equal rights and treatment for all people
vocab.example: "Coming from an egalitarian context, the hierarchy felt rigid at first."

vocab.definition: impossible to translate directly into another language without losing meaning
vocab.example: "Nunchi is a Korean untranslatable — a concept with no direct English equivalent."
